d: Advance evidence for
ety: From Middle English adducen, from Latin addūcere, adductum (“to lead or bring to”), from ad- + dūcere (“to lead”). See duke, and compare adduct.
s: At this juncture, he sought to establish the awareness of the activity; to that end, he then adduced the receipts from the transactions of June 30th.

d: A selection of passages from different authors that is compiled as an aid in learning a language
ety: From New Latin chrēstomathia, from Ancient Greek χρηστομάθεια (khrēstomátheia, “desire for learning; book containing a summary of useful knowledge or select passages,”).
s: EC Bridgman's Chinese Chrestomathy in the Canton Dialect (1841)

d: (of a leaf or bean shape) resembling the shape of kidney
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin rēnis (the genitive singular of rēn (“kidney”); see further at that entry) + English -form (suffix meaning ‘having the form or shape of’), modelled after New Latin rēnifōrmis (“of seeds: kidney-shaped”).
s: Nothing could be more simple than the furniture. The chairs were either posts mounted on four legs spread out for a base, or three-legged stools with reniform seats.

d: Completely sealed; completely airtight
ety: From Medieval Latin hermeticus, irregular derivation of Hermes Trismegistus, the god and mythological alchemist, said to possess a magic ability to seal treasure chests so that nothing could access their contents.
s: In other words, it is a mistake to regard this or any film text 'as if it were merely hermetic', or an isolated island.

d: Walk around something
s: Circumambulate the city of a dreamy Sabbath afternoon.

d: A correction by emending; a correction resulting from critical editing
ety: From Middle English emendatioun, from Latin ēmendātiō; equivalent to emend + -ation. Piecewise doublet of amendation.
s: The book might be improved by judicious emendations.

d: An indication of approved or superior status
ety: Borrowed from French cachet, first appearing in Scottish English, from 1630.
s: I remember when this diner was a quiet hangout, but lately it seems to be losing its cachet.

d: A fine coating of oxide on the surface of a metal
ety: Borrowed from Italian patina, from Latin patina (“dish, pan”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πατάνη (patánē), either from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread”) or from Pre-Greek. Doublet of paten, patena, patine, and (possibly) pan.
s: He enjoys a patina of respect by the police, despite being an ex-criminal.

d: An expert manner of speaking involving control of voice and gesture
ety: From Middle English elocucioun, ellocucioun, from Late Latin ēlocutiōnem. Doublet of elocutio.
s: His elocution was precise and clear.

d: Intelligence achieved far ahead of normal developmental schedules
ety: From French précocité.
s: How can we explain the relative precocity in political studies that the Greeks demonstrated in contrast to the backwardness of other early peoples?

d: Feeling or expressing pain or sorrow for sins or offenses
ety: From Middle English ruful, rewful. By surface analysis, rue + -ful.
s: Merely, he received it with the rueful indulgence that he would show towards Tom when he came through with one of his solutions for ending world poverty or the arms race.

d: Absorbing moisture (as from the air)
ety: From French hygroscopique.
s: All fertilizers tested are drillable at relative humidities below 50 per cent, but no fertilizer remains drillable when exposed to a humidity above its hygroscopic point.

d: Light teasing repartee
ety: Borrowed from French raillerie.
s: Excitement instantly seized the whole party: a running fire of raillery and jests was proceeding when Sam returned.

d: Demand as being one’s due or property; assert one’s right or title to
ety: From Latin arrogātus, perfect passive participle of adrogō, arrogō (“ask of, adopt, appropriate, assume”), from ad (“to”) + rogō (“ask”).
s: What is remarkable about the challenged statute and rules is not that they address medical treatments with both risks and benefits but that they arrogate to the state the right to make that decision.

d: Incapable of being transgressed or dishonored
ety: From Middle French inviolable, from Latin inviolābilis (“untouchable”), from violō (“violate”). Equivalent to in- + violable. Piecewise doublet of unviolable.
s: "Now, Mr. Jones, having obtained your promise of inviolable secrecy, I come down to the essential point."

d: Drooping without elasticity; wanting in stiffness
ety: Borrowed from Latin flaccid(us).
s: The flaccid economy of the 1970s rendered Americans even more hostile toward liberal welfare policies.

d: A silk or silklike fabric with crosswise ribs
ety: Borrowed from French gros-grain (“coarse grain, a strong fabric”), from gros (“coarse”) + grain (“grain”). Doublet of grogram, which was borrowed earlier.
s: He was on a leash, I realized. The grosgrain strap was wrapped around her hand.

d: Understatement for rhetorical effect (especially when expressing an affirmative by negating its contrary)
ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin lītotēs, from Ancient Greek λιτότης (litótēs, literally “plainness”), from λιτός (litós, “simple”).
s: Saying `I was not a little upset' when you mean `I was very upset' is an example of litotes.

d: An arrangement of flowers that is usually given as a present
ety: From Late Middle English nōsegai (?), from nōse (“nose”) (from Old English nosu, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nas- (“nose”)) + gai (“a bright or gay object; an ornament”) (from Old French gai (“cheerful, gay, happy”)); equivalent to nose + gay.
s: Tacked to Miss Trixie's desk was a large sign that said miss trixie with an old-fashioned nosegay drawn in crayon in one corner.

d: Planned in advance
ety: From afore- + thought.
s: This act was not merely wrong; it was clearly done with malice aforethought.

d: Battleship that has big guns all of the same caliber
ety: Named after HMS Dreadnought, the first battleship finished of this type, itself named for Etymology 2.
s: Herbert steering the dreadnought limousine through the night, black cap on his black head.

d: Charge falsely or with malicious intent; attack the good name and reputation of someone
ety: From Middle English besmorchen (attested in besmorchid). Compare Middle English bismotered (“bespattered, soiled”). By surface analysis, be- + smirch.
s: The newspaper was on a campaign to besmirch the actor.

d: A sudden and decisive change of government illegally or by force
ety: Borrowed from German Putsch, from Alemannic German Putsch (“knock, thrust, blow”), of imitative origin.
s: Afterward, the ringleaders of the failed putsch were publicly executed.

d: Declare to be
ety: From Middle English ajugen, adjugen, from Old French ajugier, from Latin adiudicare. Doublet of adjudicate.
s: City felt they were victims of an injustice after 16 minutes when Silva's free-kick floated straight in, but French official Stephane Lannoy adjudged that Joleon Lescott had fouled keeper Jorg Butt.

d: Confer dignity or honor upon
ety: From Middle English ennoblen, from Old French ennoblir. Equivalent to en- + noble.
s: We’d like to believe that suffering instructs and ennobles.

d: Spotlessly clean and fresh
ety: From un- + sullied.
s: Preëminently is the Lake District suited for the jaded and worn, who seek in solitude and amidst scenery unmoiled and unsullied by human artifice, refreshment alike of body and spirit.

d: Accompanied by bloodshed
ety: From Middle English sanguinarie, from Latin sanguinārius.
s: We may not propagate religion by wars, or by sanguinary persecutions to force consciences.

d: A decorated bier on which a coffin rests in state during a funeral
ety: Borrowed from French catafalque, from Italian catafalco, from Vulgar Latin *catafalicum, from Ancient Greek κατά (katá, “down”) + Latin fala (“scaffolding, wooden siege tower”), which is from Etruscan. Also influenced scaffold.
s: Until noon, the hour of the funeral, crowds continued to file by the plain pine coffin on its plain flower-covered catafalque.

d: A woman’s fur shoulder cape with hanging ends; often consisting of the whole fur of a fox or marten
ety: From Middle English tippet, Old English tæppet, from Latin tapete (“cloth”).
s: Drygoods shops did not have much that was Christmassy to display except red flannel and rabbit fur baby coats and muffs and tippets.

d: An irregular arrangement of patches of color
ety: 1670-80. Probably back-formation from motley.
s: The most common symptom is a mild mottle on the youngest leaves of infected plants.

d: A cowboy of the South American pampas
ety: Borrowed from Spanish gaucho, of uncertain origin.
s: Theirs was the spirit which upheld Darwin among the gauchos of the Argentine or Wallace among the head-hunters of Malaya.

d: Draw a line around
ety: From Latin circumscrībō, from circum (“around”) + scrībō (“write”). By surface analysis, circum- + scribe.
s: He drew a circle around the points.

d: A person who operates a farm
ety: From Middle English husbandman, husbondman, equivalent to husband + -man.
s: The husbandman must labour before he receives the fruits

d: Someone who constantly criticizes in a petty way
ety: From carp + -er.
s: He censures everything, this zealous carper.

d: Characterized by undue haste and lack of thought or deliberation; (‘brainish’ is archaic)
ety: From Middle English impetuous, from Old French impetueux, from Late Latin impetuōsus (“violent”), from Latin impetus (“attack, violence”).
s: He stands, and views in the faint rays Far, far below, the torrent's rising surge, And listens to the wild impetuous roar

d: A vocal passage of narrative text that a singer delivers with natural rhythms of speech
ety: From Italian recitativo, from recitare, from Latin recitō.
s: In Gilbert and Sullivan's Patience, Bunthorne performs the recitative "Am I Alone and Unobserved?" before going on to his solo aria "If You're Anxious For To Shine".

d: An investor who deliberately decides to go against the prevailing wisdom of other investors
ety: From contrary + -an (suffix forming agent nouns; and meaning of or pertaining to forming adjectives), modelled after words like libertarian.
s: Hello, he lied / Like velvet, this magician's sleight of tongue and hand / Hello, he lied / Beware, belie his smile / As warm and calculated as heroin / Beware the contrarian

d: A ball at which young ladies are presented to society
ety: First use appears c. 1750, in the sense of the dance, from French cotillon (“petticoat”), extended to the dance because of the distinctive lift of dress revealing the petticoat, from cotte (“dress”) + -illon (diminutive). Said to derive from the then-popular song Ma commère, quand je danse, mon cotillion va-t-il bien.
s: But now, WASP's want their place in the multicultural sun. Social rituals are social rituals. If there is Kwanzaa, why not cotillions?

d: Subsist on a meager allowance
ety: From Scots scrimp (“meager”), from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German schrimpen (“to shrivel up, wrinkle”), from Old Dutch *scrimpan, from Frankish *skrimpan, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skrimpaną (“to shrink”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off”), related to Old English sċrimman (“to shrink”) and sċrincan (“to shrivel up”). Doublet of shrink, shrimp, and shrim.
s: The company scrimped on the design so badly that it ended up defective.

d: Disarrange or rumple; dishevel
ety: From Middle English touselen, equivalent to touse + -le. Cognate with German Low German tuseln, Bavarian zusseln, züsseln.
s: The strong wind tousled my hair.
